fix: humanized scroll overshoot correction causes infinite loop

The overshoot scroll correction function has a loop that expects the
covered distance always reaches the target distance in some iteration of
the loop. That is not the case. A randomly sampled initial velocity
could be too low to cover the correction distance. This will ultimately
cause an infinite loop. The initial velocity must be derived from the
distance to guarantee that convergence. This commit is expected to solve
this problem by taking the distance into account when generating a
random initial velocity.

test: use ThreadingHTTPServer for browser-facing test servers

Single-threaded http.server.HTTPServer blocks its only thread in
rfile.readline() on the first connection it accepts. Chrome (especially under
--site-per-process) opens speculative/preconnect sockets without immediately
sending a request, so the server can stall on an idle socket and never serve the
real page request — Page.navigate then hangs the full 60s and fails with
CommandExecutionTimeout (seen on Windows CI for the cross-origin OOPIF test).
Switch every browser-facing test server to ThreadingHTTPServer so each
connection gets its own thread and idle/speculative sockets can't starve real
requests.

test: de-flake HAR in-flight/pending tests via deterministic units

Two HAR tests raced the recorder's own event processing: they left the record()
context the instant a *separate* listener saw loadingFinished/requestWillBeSent,

removed the callbacks and flushed the request as a status-0 pending entry
(observed on Windows CI: the in-flight-body test got None for status=200).

finalized (observable outcome, no race), and move the stop-time guarantees —
awaiting in-flight body tasks and flushing still-pending requests as status 0 —
to deterministic unit tests (tests/unit/test_har_recorder.py) that drive

fix(fingerprint): stop the override from rewriting Chrome's header order

Chrome writes a header where DevTools asks it to, not where it writes its
own, so every request of a profiled session carried an order no stock
browser emits. Measured against a stock Chrome 152 on the same server:
acceptLanguage on setUserAgentOverride moved accept-language from last to
just after user-agent on navigation and into the middle of the sec-ch-ua
block on subresources, and the Fetch rewrite of the worker and service
worker scripts moved both headers again. Cloudflare's detection IDs and
Akamai's request anomalies both name header order.

The identity is now left to the launch switches whenever they already
carry it. Accept-Language rides on the override only when the browser was
launched with a different list, and the mismatch is logged with the call
that avoids it. When the switches carry the reduced User-Agent and the
languages, the profile claims this host's platform and it declares no
Client Hints of its own, the User-Agent override, the worker overrides
and the browser-level Fetch interception are all skipped: Chrome then
writes every request itself, and the brands it derives are the profile's
because the major already matches the binary. A cross-platform profile,
or one with Client Hints, keeps the override and pays the order.

The Fetch rewrite, when it does run, now swaps the values where the
headers already sit instead of appending them, since continueRequest
sends exactly the list it is given.

inner_* from a profile that does not fit produced innerHeight greater
than outerHeight, which no browser reports. The profile's own chrome

Four contradictions our scanner reads on a profiled session, each one
internal to the browser and needing no reference database to spot.

AudioContext reported a baseLatency of 256/44100 next to a sampleRate of
48000: the latency Chrome computed from the real device, beside the rate
the profile claims. The host's buffer is now re-expressed in the claimed
rate, so the pair is a whole buffer again.

so 60 macOS families answered present under a Windows profile while the
layout engine rendered none of them. The profile's font list now governs
the answer, and a family the host genuinely lacks keeps Chrome's own
rejection instead of being forced to resolve.

The clone guard covered structuredClone and postMessage but not
history.pushState, history.replaceState, the data of a Notification, or
another realm's structuredClone, so nine of forty sinks cloned an object
a real browser refuses. Foreign realms are recognised by source string,
the same way the toString hook already works, with no shared state.

COMPRESSED_TEXTURE_FORMATS listed the astc, etc1, etc2 and pvrtc families
whose extensions the context no longer advertises, which ANGLE's D3D11
backend cannot expose at all: reading an extension to hide it enables it
inside Chrome, so the enum list is now filtered to what stays advertised.

The WebGL profile also gains the eight parameters that were answering the
host: uniform components per stage and combined, varying components, the
uniform buffer offset alignment, the texture LOD bias and the transform
feedback components, with D3D11 and Metal values in the examples and the
two GLES identities asserted in tests. WEBGL_debug_shaders stops being
hidden unconditionally, since almost every Windows machine exposes it;
the profile decides, and the example says when to drop it.

feat(fingerprint): hide the Web APIs the claimed OS does not implement

Chrome exposes an interface only where the platform can back it, so the set
of APIs a browser has is a statement about its host, and CreepJS reads it.
A Windows profile on this Mac answered with BarcodeDetector, which needs a
platform barcode backend Windows has none of; an Android profile answered
with SharedWorker, WebHID, Web Serial and audio output selection, none of
which Chrome for Android ships.

The profile gains a platform_apis section listing what to remove, as dotted
paths resolved from the global scope, and the builder deletes each one where
it is actually defined, own property or prototype, in the page and in every
worker. Removing is all a profile can do honestly: an API the host does not
implement cannot be conjured, so an Android profile run from a desktop still
answers without the Contact Picker and the Content Index, and the example
says so.

The three shipped profiles carry the lists for their claimed OS, sourced
from the same table the scanner grades against.

decode, which is a statement about the build and the operating system. A
Chromium without the proprietary codecs answers '' for H.264 and AAC where
Google Chrome answers 'probably', and HEVC decodes on macOS and Windows while
a Linux build refuses it. A cross-OS profile that left both untouched
contradicted the platform it claimed, on a surface a page reads with two
calls; the hCaptcha payload traced on 2026-09-16 called them 36 times.

with whitespace, quotes and case normalised so any spelling of the same type
matches. The native method runs first on every call, so the receiver check,

value is replaced. A type outside the map keeps the browser's own answer,
which makes a partial map safe. Existence guards let the same script cover
the page and the workers, where MediaSource exists and HTMLMediaElement does
not.

asking for HEVC 'probably' and VP9 '' flipped both, MediaSource for H.264
went to false, and every type left out of the map kept its native answer.

The three example profiles carry the codec map of the system they declare,
with HEVC present on Windows and macOS and refused on Linux.

The twelve content types are the ones the hCaptcha payload actually queries,
recovered by deobfuscating its script and reading its own string table. The

trixie answer all twelve identically, so the set does not separate one desktop
OS from another and the three desktop profiles share one map. What it does
separate is browser family and a Chromium built without proprietary codecs.

feat(fingerprint): cover the WebGL limits the hCaptcha payload actually asks for

parameters it queries in one sweep: 47 of them, covering WebGL 1 and WebGL 2
limits together. WebGLProfile could declare 33. The five that carry identity
and were missing are now in the map: SUBPIXEL_BITS, MAX_ELEMENTS_VERTICES,

Of the nine still outside, four are the masked VENDOR, RENDERER, VERSION and

constants, and four are stencil masks, which are pipeline state rather than a
statement about the device.

One existing entry was misnamed and the duplicate key exposed it: 0x8C8A is
MAX_TRANSFORM_FEEDBACK_SEPARATE_ATTRIBS, not the interleaved component limit,
which is 0x8C80. A profile setting the old name was writing the right value to
the wrong parameter name and leaving the interleaved limit at the host value.

The point is coherence across one sweep: a profile that declares a texture
size and leaves the neighbouring limits at the backend's own numbers puts two
disagreeing answers in the same reply.

feat(examples): add a Linux desktop profile shaped for a container

The example set had Windows, macOS and Android and no Linux, which is the one
platform a container can actually be. This profile is built for that case and
its shape comes from measurement, not from copying a desktop profile.

The webgl section is deliberately absent. A container without a render node
rasterises in software, and the real ceiling there is MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE of 8192.
Declaring a modern GPU, which reports 16384, creates a contradiction any page
finds in three lines: ask for a texture the size the context just announced and
read the error. With no section the limits stay the backend's own, everything
declared can be delivered, and no self-contradiction is left. Renaming the
renderer without touching capabilities belongs to the image, through the ANGLE
environment variables, not to a profile.

Two shapes were tried and reverted, both measured. Dropping client_hints makes
the applier derive the full version from the reduced User-Agent and announce
152.0.0.0 as a build, which no Chrome reports. Installing metric-compatible
substitutes for Windows families puts Calibri in front of the layout engine,
and a Linux profile that resolves a Windows marker is worse than one that
resolves none.

Audited with the project's own scanner inside a Debian trixie container, on a
virtual display with software WebGL, a cpuset-bound CPU and the timezone in the
process environment: 6 mismatch, 18 warn, 102 ok. Two of the six are the
JavaScript floor (every injected getter leaves a stack frame and a constructor
tell), one is the host architecture disagreeing with the profile, two share the
worker-script header order as a root cause, and one is system-ui, which Chrome
resolves internally.

fix(examples): declare WebGL on the Linux container profile

The first version of this profile left the webgl section out, arguing that
declaring a limit above what the rasteriser delivers is a contradiction the
allocation test finds. That is true against an auditor that allocates, and the
project's own scanner allocates. It is not true against the payload the profile
exists to face.

Deobfuscating that payload settles it. Its string table carries the whole draw
pipeline, createShader through drawArrays with TRIANGLE_STRIP, and it reads the
result back with canvas.toDataURL. What the table does not carry is texImage2D,

tries to allocate anything at the limit it just read. The 47 enums it sweeps
are read and never verified, so the profile can answer them.

The values come from a real Mesa GL backend measured on 2026-09-16 rather than
from an invented table, because those 47 are read in one sweep and the
per-stage and combined limits relate to each other arithmetically; copying a
real vector keeps that arithmetic standing.

backend reported MAX_COMBINED_UNIFORM_BLOCKS 45 with 15 per stage, and

leaking into a WebGL context that exposes only vertex and fragment.

Shader precision is declared as desktop GL answers it, the high range at every
precision. Measured: a Chrome on real hardware promotes mediump to [127, 127,
23] while a software container answers a true [15, 15, 10], and the payload
reads getShaderPrecisionFormat 16 times while declaring precision mediump float
in its own shader.

Known gap, written into the profile: nothing here was measured against a
physical Intel UHD 620, and max_elements_vertices and max_samples still carry
the software backend's signature.

A Chromium with a brand announces itself. Brave exposes navigator.brave, whose
isBrave() answers true, and Opera exposes window.opr. A profile claiming Google
Chrome needs neither to exist, and the getOwnPropertyNames sweep the hCaptcha
collector runs 52 times finds either without effort.

Without a profile the Brave build gives itself away through three channels: the
brand in userAgentData, the navigator.brave global, and the plugin names. With

The paths live in their own constant rather than in the OS list, because they
say which browser this is and not which system it runs on. window.opr is not
measured: there is no Opera build for this architecture, and deleting a path
that does not exist is a no-op, so listing it costs nothing.

What the profile does not reach, written into the constant: navigator.plugins
still separates the two, because Brave's farbling randomises the plugin names
and they change between runs. FingerprintConfig has no plugins section.

native path. Indexed access, named access, item(), namedItem(), refresh() and

plugin that enables it, which is how Chrome relates the two arrays.

_reconcile_clamped_window rebuilt setDeviceMetricsOverride with
mobile=False and include_screen_size=True hardcoded, so the second
override contradicted the first one _apply_native_overrides had just
sent with mobile=mobile and include_screen_size=not headless.

not fit the display: the first override goes out with mobile=True and
the reconcile followed it with mobile=False, silently dropping mobile
emulation for the rest of the session. The clamp is the case where a
profile is already under strain, which is the worst moment to also
lose the viewport semantics it asked for.

Both values now travel from _apply_native_overrides through
_apply_window_bounds to the reconcile, so the second command can only
agree with the first. The include_screen_size half is not reproducible
here (a headless window is not clamped by a display, so the path never
runs), but hardcoding it had the same shape: in headless the profile
asks for no screen-size override precisely because the virtual screen
already carries it, and the reconcile would have forced it back.

an empty mapping pins nothing. _launch_identity_covers_page tested for
the key instead of its contents, so the same empty mapping claimed the
profile had Client Hints of its own and forced the User-Agent override.

That override is the thing the function exists to avoid: with one
active, Chrome writes user-agent where DevTools asks rather than where
it writes its own, so the session carries a header order no stock
browser emits. A profile paid that price for a mapping that overrides
nothing.

Checked live against Chrome 153 with the launch switches matching the
profile: an absent client_hints and an empty one now both leave the
headers to Chrome, while a populated one still takes the override path.

fix(examples): complete the Android uniform families and enforce it

The module docstring of the example tests says a profile that overrides
part of a family and lets the rest fall back to the host GPU is caught
by arithmetic alone. The vector test did not enforce that: it compared
the 4x relation only when both members were present, so a profile
declaring one member and omitting the other passed.

The Android profile was that case. It set max_vertex_uniform_vectors
256 and max_fragment_uniform_vectors 224 while both component limits
fell through to whatever the host GPU reports, which on any desktop is
not 1024 and 896. A detector reading a vector limit and its component
limit from one context sees the pair disagree.

The test now requires both members or neither, in the same shape the
combined-family test already used, and the Android profile carries the
components its vectors imply.

fix(fingerprint): correct the transform-feedback enum mapping

The three transform-feedback keys were mapped to each other's enums, a
rotation introduced when this map gained the WebGL2 limits. Read back
from a real WebGL2 context, the constants are SEPARATE_COMPONENTS
0x8C80, INTERLEAVED_COMPONENTS 0x8C8A and SEPARATE_ATTRIBS 0x8C8B; the
map held 0x8C80, 0x8C8B and 0x8C8A against interleaved,
separate-components and separate-attribs respectively.

Every configured value therefore overrode a neighbour. Setting the
three to 1111, 2222 and 3333 and reading them back through
getParameter returned 3333, 1111 and 2222; it now returns each value
under the name that set it.

A profile copying a real GPU's vector was the worst case: the three
hold an arithmetic relation, so rotating them broke it and handed a
detector the contradiction the copied vector existed to avoid.

fix(fingerprint): give a patched method the native arity, not the callback's

_patchM pinned the wrapper's length to the length of the callback it
was handed, so every caller had to remember to declare the same
parameter count as the method it replaces. _guardClone does not: it
passes one `function (value)` for all of structuredClone, the
postMessage family and History.pushState / replaceState.

Measured on Chrome 153: those two are the only ones whose native
length is 2, so with a profile applied they reported 1 while every
other guarded method happened to match. Function.length is an own
property of the function and is compared against a known value as
cheaply as toString is.

The wrapper now takes the arity from the method being replaced and
falls back to the callback's only when there is nothing to replace, so
a caller cannot get this wrong. _guardClone is unchanged.

fix(fingerprint): check the font names a local() source asks for

The FontFace.load gate authorised a probe by this.family, which the
page chooses freely, and never looked at the names inside the local()
source, which are what the browser actually resolves. A probe that
picked any allow-listed family could then name any font it liked and
read the host's true answer.

Measured with the Linux container profile on a macOS host:
new FontFace('Helvetica Neue', 'local("Helvetica Neue")') rejected as
the profile intends, while new FontFace('Arial', 'local("Helvetica
Neue")') resolved and reported a font no Linux box has. Arial is on
the profile's list, so nothing stopped the second form.

The gate now parses every local() operand and only defers to the
native load when all of them are on the list; sources carrying url()
keep native handling as before. The naive probe is unaffected, since
its family and its operand are the same name.

fix(fingerprint): stop warning about the User-Agent the header path requires

The warning compared a --user-agent option against the profile's
user_agent as written, which is the four-part build. The only value
that lets _launch_identity_matches leave the header order to Chrome is
the reduced string, because that is what Chrome exposes and puts on
the wire; the four-part build lives in the profile because the full
version feeds the Client Hints.

The two spellings are never equal, so the single option value that
reaches the header-order path was also the one value guaranteed to log
"don't combine --user-agent with apply_fingerprint". Measured with a
shipped profile: the reduced form logged the warning, the full form
did not and did not reach the path either.

The warning now accepts either spelling of the profile's own identity
and still fires for a User-Agent that is neither.

perf: stop sleeping where the browser has already answered

Three fixed delays made pydoll look slow next to Playwright on the same
Chrome and the same page, measured with a local benchmark (median ms):

  wait for an element that appears after 100 ms   506 -> 170  (Playwright 185)
  find + click                                     108 -> 1.4  (Playwright 33)
  find + clear + type 30 characters               4473 -> 13   (Playwright 9)

Polling loops in find(), wait_until(), get_shadow_root() and
find_shadow_roots() slept a fixed half second between attempts; they now
start at 20 ms and back off to 250 ms, so a quick outcome is quick and a
long wait still polls cheaply. A plain click no longer holds the button
for 100 ms, a plain type_text no longer holds each key for 80 ms and
pauses 50 ms between characters, and no longer re-focuses the element
per keystroke, and press() no longer holds the key for 100 ms. Human
timing is what humanize=True is for, and that path is unchanged.

perf: faster stop, quicker readiness poll, and log calls that cost nothing when off

browser.stop() slept a fixed 100 ms after terminating the process, on top

plus close measures 376 ms against 481 ms before (Playwright: 425 ms on

On the per-command path every debug and info log call formatted an
f-string even though the default level discards it; 157 log calls in the
connection, browser, tab, element and interaction modules now pass their
arguments to the logger, which formats only when the level is enabled.
A raw command round trip is 0.122 ms against a 0.149 ms raw websocket
floor measured with a separate client, down from 0.175 to 0.200 ms.

perf: send a typed string's key events as one batch

ConnectionHandler.execute_commands() sends a sequence of commands without
waiting for each answer and then collects all the answers; the browser
processes one session's commands in order, so keydown and keyup stay
ordered while the whole string costs a single round trip. Plain
type_text() builds the keydown/keyup pair for every character and sends
the list through the element's routing, so a batch inside an iframe still
carries the frame's session id. Typing 30 characters measures 3.9 ms,
down from 13 ms after the previous change (Playwright: 8.9 ms with
press_sequentially on the same Chrome).

The fake connection used by unit tests mirrors the new method, and the
connection handler's integration tests check that a batch reaches the
server in order and comes back in order. The Playwright page-error test
now polls for the event instead of waiting a fixed 200 ms, which was too
short under four workers.

exits, and the error names the exit code or the timeout, the port and

fix: retry hook arity from its signature, and sync runtime fork, cancel and cache fixes

The retry decorator decided whether on_retry takes the instance by
matching the text of a caught TypeError, so a TypeError raised inside a
one-argument callback triggered a second, argument-less call. The form
now comes from the callback's signature; builtins without one, such as
dict.clear, are called without arguments.

In the sync runtime, the after-fork hook reset the singleton by taking
the lock the child inherited, which deadlocks when another parent thread
held it at the fork; the child now replaces both instance and lock
without acquiring anything. run() cancels the scheduled coroutine when
waiting fails, so a timeout or interruption no longer leaves it running
on the loop. Wrapped handlers are cached per runtime, so a wrapper made
before a shutdown, bound to that runtime's dispatch executor, is not
handed to the runtime that replaces it.
